recipes.name: Foil-Packet Hamburger Dinners
recipes.summary: The classic campfire supper: a seasoned beef patty on sliced potatoes, carrots and onion, sealed in foil and cooked in the coals.
steps: At home or at camp: mix the beef with half the salt, the pepper and garlic powder, and shape 4 patties about ¾ inch thick. Wash your hands before and after handling raw meat; bring soap and water, or wipes, if there’s no tap (USDA).

Tear four sheets of heavy-duty foil about 18 inches long. (Or double up regular foil.) Divide the potatoes, carrots and onion among them, sprinkle with the rest of the salt and dot with butter. Lay a patty on top.
Bring the long sides of the foil together and fold them down twice, then fold the ends in tightly, so the steam stays in.

Cook over a bed of glowing coals in an established fire ring or on a camp grill, not over tall flames. Use long tongs and heat-proof gloves, and open packets away from your face: the steam is very hot. Cook 30 to 40 minutes, turning the packets over halfway.
Open one packet carefully and check: the potatoes should be tender and the beef should read 160°F in the center (USDA). If not, reseal it and cook 5 minutes more.
recipes.make_ahead: Shape the patties and slice the vegetables at home; assemble the packets and keep them flat in the cooler, below everything else, for up to 1 day.

freezer.text: Freeze assembled packets flat; they help keep the cooler cold and thaw by the second night. Thaw in the cooler, not on the table.

leftovers.text: Leftovers are safe only while the cooler still has ice; otherwise throw them out (USDA). Pack out all trash and food scraps (Leave No Trace).

recipes.kids: Kids can layer their own packets with clean hands and help fold the edges. A grown-up handles the coals.

swaps.stove: No fire? Cook the packets on a camp grill over medium heat, or in a covered skillet on the camp stove.
swaps.turkey: Use ground turkey and cook to 165°F.

prep_day.ahead: Shape the patties and slice the vegetables.

recipes.name: Foil-Packet Italian Chicken and Vegetables
recipes.summary: Chunks of chicken with zucchini, peppers and onion, olive oil and Italian herbs, cooked in foil packets over the coals.
steps: At home, put the chicken in a sealed container or zip-top bag with half the oil, the seasoning, garlic powder and salt. Put the vegetables in another bag with the rest of the oil and the pepper. Keep the raw meat in the cooler at 40°F or below, sealed and packed below ready-to-eat food, until it goes on the fire (USDA).

Tear four sheets of heavy-duty foil about 18 inches long. (Or double up regular foil.) Divide the vegetables and chicken among them. Fold the long sides together twice and crimp the ends. Wash your hands before and after handling raw meat; bring soap and water, or wipes, if there’s no tap (USDA).

Cook over a bed of glowing coals in an established fire ring or on a camp grill, not over tall flames. Use long tongs and heat-proof gloves, and open packets away from your face: the steam is very hot. Cook 20 to 25 minutes, turning once.
Open one packet carefully and check the biggest piece of chicken: it must read 165°F (USDA). Sprinkle with Parmesan.
recipes.make_ahead: Cut and season everything at home the day before; it marinates in the cooler.

freezer.text: Freeze the seasoned raw chicken flat in its bag; it doubles as an ice pack and thaws in the cooler by day 2.

leftovers.text: Leftovers are safe only while the cooler still has ice; otherwise throw them out (USDA). Pack out all trash and food scraps (Leave No Trace).

recipes.kids: Kids can toss the vegetables with oil and build the packets.

swaps.rice: Serve over instant rice made on the camp stove.
swaps.shrimp: Use peeled shrimp and cook 8 to 10 minutes, until opaque.

prep_day.ahead: Cut and season the chicken and vegetables.

recipes.name: Foil-Packet Sausage, Potatoes and Corn
recipes.summary: Smoked sausage, little potatoes, corn on the cob and green beans with butter and paprika. Like a shrimp boil without the pot.
steps: At home, microwave or boil the halved potatoes 5 minutes, until just starting to soften, so they finish in the fire with everything else. Cool and pack them in the cooler.
Toss the potatoes, corn, green beans and sausage with the butter, paprika, garlic powder and salt.
Tear four sheets of heavy-duty foil about 18 inches long. (Or double up regular foil.) Divide everything among them and seal: long sides folded together twice, ends crimped.

Cook over a bed of glowing coals in an established fire ring or on a camp grill, not over tall flames. Use long tongs and heat-proof gloves, and open packets away from your face: the steam is very hot. Cook 25 to 35 minutes, turning once, until the potatoes are tender. Smoked sausage is already cooked; heat it until steaming, 165°F (USDA).
recipes.make_ahead: Par-cook the potatoes and cut the corn at home.

leftovers.text: Leftovers are safe only while the cooler still has ice; otherwise throw them out (USDA). Pack out all trash and food scraps (Leave No Trace).

recipes.kids: Kids can shuck and help cut the corn (with a grown-up) and fill the packets.

swaps.veggie: Use plant-based sausage, or a drained can of chickpeas.

recipes.name: Campfire Banana Boats
recipes.summary: A banana split in its peel, stuffed with chocolate chips and marshmallows and warmed in the coals until gooey. Eat it with a spoon.

ingredients.prep: cut in half, or 1 cup minis

steps: With the peel on, cut a slit down the inside curve of each banana, through the fruit but not the bottom peel. Open it a little to make a pocket.
Stuff the pocket with chocolate chips and marshmallows. Wrap each banana in foil.
Set them on the grate or at the edge of the coals for 5 to 8 minutes, until the chocolate melts.
Let them cool 2 minutes before opening; melted marshmallow is very hot. Top with graham crumbs and eat from the peel with a spoon.
recipes.make_ahead: Pack the fillings in a bag at home.
recipes.kids: Kids can stuff their own. A grown-up handles the coals.

swaps.smores: Make classic s’mores from scratch too.

credits.name: Campfire (Grokipedia)

recipes.name: Campfire Dutch-Oven Chili
recipes.summary: A big pot of beef and bean chili, simmered over the fire or a camp stove. Warms everyone up on a cool night.
equipment: 12-inch cast-iron Dutch oven or large pot
steps: At home, chop the onion and pepper and mix the spices in a small bag. Keep the raw meat in the cooler at 40°F or below, sealed and packed below ready-to-eat food, until it goes on the fire (USDA).

Set the Dutch oven on a grate over the fire (or a camp stove over medium-high heat) and add the oil. Brown the beef with the onion and pepper, breaking it up, 8 to 10 minutes, until no pink remains and it reads 160°F (USDA). Spoon off extra fat into a can to pack out.
Stir in the spices, then the beans, tomatoes and tomato sauce.
Bring to a simmer, then move the pot to a cooler part of the grate (or turn the stove to low). Cover and simmer 30 to 40 minutes, stirring every 10 minutes so it doesn’t catch on the bottom.
Serve with cheese, over walking-taco chips or with bannock.
recipes.make_ahead: Make the chili at home, cool it fast in shallow containers, and freeze it flat in bags. It keeps the cooler cold; reheat to 165°F at camp.

leftovers.text: Refrigerate (or ice) leftovers within 2 hours, within 1 hour above 90°F, and keep them only while the cooler has ice (USDA). Reheat to 165°F.

recipes.kids: Kids can open the cans (with a grown-up) and stir the pot away from the flames.

swaps.veggie: Skip the beef and add a third can of beans plus a can of corn.

prep_day.ahead: Make it at home and freeze it flat.

recipes.name: Camp Skillet Breakfast Hash
recipes.summary: Bacon, crispy hash browns, peppers and onion in one big skillet, with eggs cooked right on top. Breakfast for the whole campsite.
equipment: 12-inch cast-iron skillet with a lid (or foil)

ingredients.prep: kept in the cooler; thawed is fine

steps: Cook the bacon in the skillet over medium heat until crisp. Lift it out, leaving about 2 tablespoons of fat in the pan. Pour the rest into a can to cool and pack out.
Add the hash browns, onion and pepper. Spread them out and leave them alone 5 minutes to brown, then stir and cook 8 to 10 minutes more, until crisp and tender. Season with salt and pepper.
Stir the bacon back in. Make 8 wells and crack an egg into each. Cover with a lid or foil and cook on low 6 to 8 minutes, until the whites and yolks are firm (USDA).
Sprinkle with cheese, cover a minute to melt it, and serve from the pan.
recipes.make_ahead: Chop the onion and pepper at home; crack the eggs into a sealed bottle or container for the cooler (use within 2 days).

leftovers.text: Leftovers are safe only while the cooler still has ice; otherwise throw them out (USDA). Pack out all trash and food scraps (Leave No Trace).

recipes.kids: Kids can crack eggs into a cup first, then slide them into the wells.

swaps.veggie: Skip the bacon and use 2 tablespoons of oil; add mushrooms or spinach.
swaps.burritos: Scoop it into tortillas for breakfast burritos.

recipes.name: Shake-and-Pour Camp Pancakes
recipes.summary: Mix the dry ingredients at home in a bottle with powdered milk. At camp, add water and oil, shake, and pour. No eggs to keep cold.
equipment: 1-quart wide-mouth bottle or jar with a tight lid
steps: At home: put the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt and dry milk in a clean, dry 1-quart bottle or jar (a funnel helps). Close it and label it “add 1½ cups water + 3 tbsp oil.”
At camp: add the water and oil, close the lid tightly and shake hard for about 30 seconds, until there are no dry pockets. A few small lumps are fine.
Heat an oiled griddle over medium-low on the camp stove. Pour ¼-cup pancakes straight from the bottle.
Cook until bubbles cover the top and the edges look dry, about 2 minutes, then flip and cook 1 to 2 minutes more, until golden and cooked through. Don’t taste the raw batter (FDA).
recipes.make_ahead: The dry mix keeps 2 months in the pantry.

freezer.text: Keep the dry mix in the pantry.

recipes.kids: Kids love to shake the bottle. Pouring and flipping on a hot griddle is a grown-up job, or for older kids with help.

swaps.blueberries: Drop a few blueberries onto each pancake after pouring.
swaps.from_scratch: Use 2 cups of the from-scratch pancake mix.

prep_day.ahead: Fill the bottle with the dry mix.

recipes.name: Dutch-Oven Peach Cobbler
recipes.summary: Canned peaches under a buttery batter, baked in a Dutch oven with coals underneath and on the lid. The classic campout dessert.
equipment: 12-inch camp Dutch oven with legs and a flat, rimmed lid
charcoal briquettes and a chimney starter

ingredients.prep: in juice, drained (save ½ cup juice)

steps: At home, mix the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt and half the cinnamon in a bag.
Light about 26 briquettes in a chimney starter in the fire ring or on bare ground cleared of anything that can burn. When they are covered in gray ash (15 to 20 minutes), they are ready.
Line the Dutch oven with foil if you like (for easy cleanup). Spread the peaches and saved juice in the bottom and sprinkle with the rest of the cinnamon.
Stir the milk and melted butter into the dry mix just until combined, and spoon the batter over the peaches.

Put on the lid. Set the oven over 9 briquettes in a ring and put 17 on the lid, spread evenly. This is about 350°F for a 12-inch oven (diameter × 2, plus 2 for each 25°F, two-thirds on top for baking).

Bake 35 to 45 minutes, turning the oven a quarter turn one way and the lid a quarter turn the other every 15 minutes so it browns evenly. Lift the lid carefully, brushing ash away, to check: the top should be golden and a knife come out clean.
Let it cool 10 minutes; the fruit is very hot. When done, put the used coals in the fire ring and put them out completely: drown, stir, drown and feel.
recipes.make_ahead: Mix the dry batter at home.

leftovers.text: Covered, it keeps overnight in the cooler while it still has ice.

recipes.kids: Kids can spoon on the batter. Coals and the lid are for grown-ups.

swaps.oven: At home, bake it in a 9-by-13-inch dish at 350°F for 40 to 45 minutes.
swaps.dry_milk: Use ¼ cup dry milk in the bag and ¾ cup water at camp, so nothing needs the cooler.

recipes.name: Campfire Bannock (Skillet or Stick)
recipes.summary: A simple flatbread of flour, baking powder, fat and water, cooked in a skillet or wrapped around a stick over the coals. A camp staple for centuries.
equipment: mixing bowl or a sturdy zip-top bag
clean green sticks or metal roasting sticks (optional)
steps: At home, mix the flour, baking powder, sugar and salt and rub in the shortening with your fingers until it looks like coarse crumbs. Pack it in a zip-top bag; it keeps 2 weeks.
At camp, add the water a little at a time, squeezing the bag or stirring in a bowl, until it makes a soft dough that isn’t sticky. Knead it a few times.

Skillet: pat the dough into a round about ¾ inch thick. Heat the oil in the skillet over low coals or a low stove flame and cook 8 to 10 minutes per side, until golden and it sounds hollow when tapped. Keep the heat low so the middle cooks before the outside burns.
On a stick: roll pieces of dough into ropes and wind them around clean sticks. Hold them over glowing coals, turning, 8 to 10 minutes, until golden and cooked through. Don’t eat raw dough (FDA).
Cut into wedges and eat warm, with butter, jam or the chili.
recipes.make_ahead: The dry mix with the fat rubbed in keeps 2 weeks in a cool place.

freezer.text: Keep the dry mix in the pantry.

leftovers.text: Wrap leftover bannock and eat it within 2 days.

recipes.kids: Kids can mix the dough in the bag and wind it on sticks. Supervise them near the fire.

swaps.sweet: Add a handful of raisins or berries and a pinch of cinnamon.
swaps.traditional: Lard is the traditional fat in many families; butter works too.

prep_day.ahead: Mix the dry ingredients and fat.

recipes.name: Walking Tacos
recipes.summary: Taco meat spooned straight into a bag of tortilla chips, topped and eaten with a fork. Hardly any dishes to wash at camp.

ingredients.prep: in 6 single-serving bags or zip-top bags

steps: Brown the beef in a skillet over medium-high heat on the camp stove, breaking it up, until no pink remains and it reads 160°F (USDA). Spoon off extra fat into a can to pack out.
Stir in the seasoning and water and simmer 5 minutes, until thick.
Crush the chips a little in each bag, open it, and spoon in the meat. Let everyone add cheese, lettuce, tomato, salsa and sour cream, then eat out of the bag with a fork.
Keep the cheese, lettuce, salsa and sour cream in the cooler until serving and put them back within 2 hours, or 1 hour on a day above 90°F (USDA).
recipes.make_ahead: Cook the taco meat at home, cool it fast and freeze it flat; reheat to 165°F at camp.

freezer.text: Freeze the cooked meat up to 3 months.

leftovers.text: Leftovers are safe only while the cooler still has ice; otherwise throw them out (USDA). Pack out all trash and food scraps (Leave No Trace).

recipes.kids: Kids can crush the chips and build their own.

swaps.veggie: Use the seasoned lentil taco filling or black beans.

prep_day.ahead: Cook and freeze the taco meat.

recipes.name: Pie-Iron Pizza Pockets
recipes.summary: Buttered bread around pizza sauce, mozzarella and pepperoni, toasted in a pie iron over the coals until crisp and melty.
steps: Butter one side of each slice of bread.
Open a pie iron and lay a slice, butter side down, in one half. Spread with 2 tablespoons of sauce, add a quarter of the cheese and 4 slices of pepperoni, and top with another slice, butter side up.
Close the iron, latch it, and trim any bread sticking out.
Hold it over glowing coals (not in the flames) 2 to 4 minutes per side, peeking once, until golden. Open it carefully: the iron and filling are very hot. Cool 2 minutes before eating.
recipes.make_ahead: Pack the fillings in small containers in the cooler.
recipes.kids: Kids can build their own pocket. A grown-up holds the hot iron.

swaps.dessert: Fill with canned pie filling or chocolate chips and marshmallows.
swaps.skillet: No pie iron? Cook them like grilled cheese in a skillet.

credits.name: Pie iron (Grokipedia)

recipes.name: One-Pot Camp Stove Mac and Cheese
recipes.summary: Macaroni cooked in just enough water to soak up, then stirred with milk, butter and cheddar. One pot, no draining.
steps: Bring the water and salt to a boil in the pot over the camp stove.
Add the macaroni and cook, stirring often, 8 to 10 minutes, until tender and most of the water is soaked up. Add a splash more water if it gets dry before the pasta is done.
Turn the heat to low and stir in the milk and butter until hot, then the cheese a handful at a time until creamy. Season with pepper.
recipes.make_ahead: Shred the cheese at home and keep it in the cooler.

leftovers.text: Leftovers are safe only while the cooler still has ice; otherwise throw them out (USDA). Pack out all trash and food scraps (Leave No Trace).

recipes.kids: Kids can stir in the cheese, standing away from the stove with a long spoon.

swaps.shelf_stable: Use a can of evaporated milk instead of fresh milk; it needs no cooler until opened.
swaps.add_ins: Stir in chopped hot dogs or leftover chili.

recipes.name: Cinnamon Sugar Biscuits on a Stick
recipes.summary: Biscuit dough twisted around a roasting stick, toasted over the coals, then rolled in butter and cinnamon sugar.
equipment: clean roasting sticks or long metal skewers
small pot or foil pan for butter
steps: Mix the sugar and cinnamon on a plate. Melt the butter in a small pot at the edge of the fire.
Roll each biscuit into a rope about 8 inches long and wind it around the end of a stick, pinching the ends.
Hold it a few inches above glowing coals, turning slowly, 8 to 12 minutes, until golden all over and cooked through; it should slide off easily and feel light. Don’t eat raw dough (FDA).
Slide it off, brush with butter and roll in cinnamon sugar. Let it cool a minute before biting.
recipes.make_ahead: Mix the cinnamon sugar at home. Keep the biscuits in the cooler.

freezer.text: Keep the dough in the cooler.

recipes.kids: Kids can roll and wind the dough and toast it, supervised, standing back from the fire with a long stick.

recipes.name: Nut-Free Camp Trail Mix
recipes.summary: Seeds, oat cereal, pretzels, raisins, cranberries and a few chocolate chips. All the crunch of trail mix, without peanuts or tree nuts.
equipment: bags or containers for each hiker
steps: Stir everything together in a big bowl.
Scoop ½-cup portions into small bags, one per hiker per snack, so nobody reaches into a shared bag with unwashed hands.
recipes.make_ahead: Keeps 1 month in a sealed container.
recipes.kids: Kids can measure, mix and bag it.

swaps.nut_free: Check the seed, cereal and chocolate labels for “may contain” warnings if someone has a severe allergy.

credits.name: Trail mix (Grokipedia)

recipes.name: Homemade Hot Cocoa Mix
recipes.summary: Powdered milk, cocoa and sugar mixed at home. At camp, stir a scoop into a mug of hot water for cocoa by the fire.
steps: Whisk the dry milk, powdered sugar, cocoa and salt together until no lumps remain, and pack it in a jar or bag.
At camp, heat safe drinking water. If your water comes from a lake or stream, bring it to a rolling boil for 1 minute first (USDA).
Stir ⅓ cup of mix into 1 cup of hot water. Let it cool to sipping temperature before handing it to kids.
recipes.make_ahead: Keeps 3 months in a sealed jar.
recipes.kids: Kids can whisk the mix and fill the jars; they make good gifts.

swaps.richer: Add ½ cup of chocolate chips, finely chopped.
